THOUGHT: The clinical picture is hundreds of small (1–2 mm), monomorphic, dark brown–black papules that began abruptly after a sunburn and slowly progressed over 4 years in a healthy, young African American woman. Lesions are widely distributed (including palms, face, tongue, sclera) and some are pruritic and removable with scratching leaving hyperpigmented macules. Laboratory and chest CT are normal. Histology shows circumscribed pigmented epithelioid melanocytic nests located mainly at the tips of rete ridges (junctional pattern), moderate cytologic atypia, pigment incontinence in the papillary dermis, no mitoses, no confluence at the dermal–epidermal junction, and only low pagetoid migration on Melan-A. These features point to multiple acquired junctional melanocytic nevi rather than melanoma. The clinical trigger (sunburn) and abrupt, widespread onset are classic for idiopathic eruptive melanocytic nevi (IEMN). The absence of mitoses, lack of confluent growth, low pagetoid spread, long stable course and monomorphous small size argue strongly against invasive melanoma. Other considerations include dysplastic (atypical) nevus syndrome, eruptive Spitz nevi, and rarer lentiginous or mucocutaneous lentigo syndromes, but these are less consistent with the combined clinicopathologic findings.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Idiopathic eruptive melanocytic nevi (eruptive junctional/acquired melanocytic nevi) — most likely
2) Multiple acquired junctional melanocytic nevi (non‑syndromic, progressive) — similar/overlapping with #1
3) Familial atypical multiple mole–melanoma syndrome (dysplastic nevus syndrome) — possible but less likely (no family history, lesions small/monomorphic)
4) Eruptive Spitz nevi (multiple Spitz/Spitz‑type proliferations) — less likely (age, distribution, absent Kamino bodies, histology not classic)
5) Multiple primary cutaneous melanomas or metastatic melanoma presenting as numerous small pigmented papules — unlikely given histology (no mitoses, lack of confluent growth, low pagetoid spread) but must be considered until clinicopathologic correlation and follow‑up confirm benign behavior.

Case Information:
An African American woman in her 30s with no medical history presented with a 4-year history of diffuse progressive proliferation of dark papules. The lesions initially began on her thighs and rapidly multiplied throughout her skin. Some lesions were pruritic and when scratched could be removed, leaving behind a hyperpigmented macule. The patient described a sunburn several weeks prior to the initial eruption. She was taking no medications and these lesions were unchanged throughout an uncomplicated pregnancy. No personal or family history of melanoma or eruptive nevi.

Physical Examination:
Hundreds of 1- to 2-mm dark brown-black monomorphic papules throughout trunk, extremities, palms, face, tongue, and sclera. No lymphadenopathy present.

Diagnostic Tests:
- Laboratory tests: Complete blood cell count and comprehensive metabolic panel were unremarkable.- Imaging studies: Computed tomography of chest was unremarkable.- Pathology:  Image Title: Punch biopsy of right arm (Figure B-C)  Image Description: Shows circumscribed proliferation of pigmented epithelioid melanocytic nests, located primarily at tips of rete ridges. Moderate cytologic atypia present. Superficial papillary dermis shows prominent pigment incontinence. No mitotic figures seen. Kamino bodies not visualized.    Image Title: Melan-A immunostain (Figure D)  Image Description: Shows low pagetoid migration of melanocytes with a lack of melanocytic confluence at the dermal-epidermal junction.
